craft.name: Apollo Lunar Module
craft.subtitle: The lander that carried astronauts to the Moon's surface

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Apollo crewed Moon landings

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 1969 (Apollo 11, first landing)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired (last flew 1972)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 7.04 m tall, 9.4 m across the landing legs

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 15,103 kg (Apollo 11 LM, fueled)

facts.label: About
facts.value: The Lunar Module was a two-part spacecraft built only to fly in space and land on the Moon. Two astronauts rode it down to the surface while a third stayed in orbit. When it was time to leave, the top half blasted off and used the bottom half as its launch pad.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It never needed to be streamlined, because it never flew through air. That is why it looks so boxy and spidery.

craft.name: Cassini-Huygens
craft.subtitle: Orbited Saturn for 13 years and dropped a probe on Titan

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Saturn orbiter and Titan probe

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, ESA, and the Italian Space Agency (ASI)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Mission ended 2017 (dove into Saturn on purpose)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 6.7 m high, 4 m wide

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 5,712 kg at launch (with fuel and the Huygens probe)

facts.label: About
facts.value: Cassini spent 13 years orbiting Saturn, studying its rings, its storms, and its moons. It carried Europe's Huygens probe, which parachuted to the surface of Titan in 2005. At the end, Cassini was steered into Saturn so it could never crash into and contaminate a moon that might host life.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Cassini found evidence of a global ocean of liquid water under the icy crust of Saturn's moon Enceladus.

craft.subtitle: A space telescope that sees the universe in X-rays

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: X-ray space telescope

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (operated by the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 1999 (Space Shuttle Columbia)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 13.8 m long, 19.5 m across the solar arrays

facts.label: About
facts.value: Chandra studies the hottest, most violent places in the universe, like exploding stars and matter falling into black holes. X-rays cannot get through Earth's air, so an X-ray telescope has to work in space. Its mirrors are shaped like nested barrels so X-rays skim off them at shallow angles.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Chandra's mirrors are among the smoothest ever made.

craft.subtitle: A car-sized science lab exploring Gale Crater on Mars

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Mars Science Laboratory

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 3 m long, 2.7 m wide, 2.2 m tall

facts.label: Mass

facts.label: About
facts.value: Curiosity is a nuclear-powered rover about the size of a small car. It drills into rocks and analyzes them in onboard labs to learn whether Mars once had conditions that could support microbes. It found that Gale Crater once held a lake of fresh water.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Curiosity was lowered to the ground on cables by a hovering rocket stage called the sky crane.

craft.subtitle: The first spacecraft to orbit two different worlds beyond Earth

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Asteroid belt orbiter (Vesta and Ceres)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Mission ended 2018 (out of fuel, still orbiting Ceres)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 19.7 m across the solar arrays

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 1,217.7 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Dawn explored the two biggest objects in the asteroid belt, Vesta and the dwarf planet Ceres. It used ion engines that push gently but for a very long time, which let it leave orbit around one world and travel to another. At Ceres it found bright salt deposits left by briny water.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Dawn's ion engines pushed with about the force of a sheet of paper resting on your hand.

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Jupiter orbiter and atmospheric probe

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL (with partners in Germany and other countries)

facts.label: Status

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Galileo's big umbrella-like antenna never fully opened, so engineers rewrote its software to send data through a much smaller antenna.

craft.name: Hubble Space Telescope
craft.subtitle: The school-bus-sized telescope orbiting Earth since 1990

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Visible and ultraviolet space telescope

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and ESA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 1990 (Space Shuttle Discovery)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 13.2 m long, 4.2 m wide

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 12,200 kg (after the last servicing mission in 2009)

facts.label: About
facts.value: Hubble orbits above the blurring effect of Earth's air, so it takes extremely sharp pictures of planets, nebulas, and galaxies. Astronauts visited it five times to repair and upgrade it. Its measurements helped show that the expansion of the universe is speeding up.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Hubble has no rocket thrusters. It turns by spinning heavy wheels inside, using Newton's third law.

craft.name: Ingenuity Mars Helicopter
craft.subtitle: The first aircraft to fly on another planet

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Mars technology demonstration (rode with Perseverance)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 2020 (first flight April 19, 2021)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Flights ended January 2024 (rotor damage)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 0.49 m tall, rotors 1.2 m tip to tip

facts.label: Mass

facts.label: About
facts.value: Ingenuity was a small solar-powered helicopter that proved powered flight is possible on Mars, where the air is about 1% as thick as Earth's. It was planned for five test flights and ended up making 72. It also scouted the terrain ahead of the Perseverance rover.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its rotor blades spun at about 2,400 revolutions per minute to get enough lift in Mars's thin air.

craft.name: James Webb Space Telescope
craft.subtitle: The largest space telescope ever launched
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: James Webb Space Telescope (A)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Infrared space telescope

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, ESA, and the Canadian Space Agency (CSA)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 2021 (Ariane 5)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: sunshield 21.2 m x 14.2 m (about a tennis court)

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 6,200 kg

facts.label: About
facts.value: Webb sees infrared light, which lets it look through dust clouds and back to some of the first galaxies that formed after the Big Bang. Its gold-coated mirror is 6.5 m across, made of 18 hexagonal segments. A five-layer sunshield keeps the telescope colder than minus 220 degrees Celsius so its own heat does not swamp the faint signals.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Webb had to unfold itself in space, like origami, because it was too big to fit inside any rocket.

craft.name: Juno
craft.subtitle: A solar-powered spacecraft orbiting Jupiter's poles

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Jupiter polar orbiter

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL (led by Southwest Research Institute)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 2011 (arrived 2016)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating in an extended mission (last confirmed mid-2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: body 3.5 m; more than 20 m across the solar arrays

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 3,625 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Juno loops over Jupiter's poles to study what is inside the giant planet, including its gravity, magnetic field, and deep atmosphere. It is the first solar-powered spacecraft sent that far from the Sun, so it needs enormous solar arrays. Its radiation vault shields its electronics from Jupiter's intense radiation.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: At Jupiter, Juno's huge solar arrays make only about 500 watts, enough for about five old-style 100-watt light bulbs. Near Earth, the same arrays would make about 14,000 watts.

craft.name: Kepler
craft.subtitle: The planet hunter that found thousands of worlds

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Exoplanet survey telescope

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired 2018 (out of fuel)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 4.7 m tall, 2.7 m wide

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 1,052.4 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Kepler stared at the same patch of sky for years, measuring the brightness of about 150,000 stars. When a planet passes in front of its star, the star dims very slightly, and Kepler watched for those dips. It showed that planets are common around other stars.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Kepler's camera was the largest NASA had ever flown in space at the time, with about 95 million pixels.

craft.name: Parker Solar Probe
craft.subtitle: The spacecraft that flies through the Sun's outer atmosphere

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Close-up study of the Sun's corona and solar wind

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (built by Johns Hopkins APL)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 3 m tall; heat shield 2.3 m across

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 685 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Parker Solar Probe dives closer to the Sun than any spacecraft before it, passing through the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona. A thick carbon heat shield always faces the Sun, keeping the instruments behind it near room temperature. It studies how the solar wind gets its speed.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: At closest approach it moves at about 700,000 km/h, the fastest speed of any human-made object.

craft.name: Perseverance Rover
craft.subtitle: Collecting rock samples in Jezero Crater on Mars

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Mars 2020: search for signs of ancient life

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026). Science is paused while engineers fix a radio problem.

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 3 m long, 2.7 m wide, 2.2 m tall

facts.label: About
facts.value: Perseverance explores an ancient river delta in Jezero Crater, looking for signs that microbes once lived on Mars. It drills rock cores and seals them in tubes for a possible future mission to bring back to Earth. It also carried the Ingenuity helicopter.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Perseverance carries two microphones. In 2021 it made the first audio recording on Mars using a microphone, capturing a Martian breeze.

craft.name: TESS
craft.subtitle: Searching the nearest, brightest stars for new planets
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) (A)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA (led by MIT)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 2018 (Falcon 9)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 3.9 m across its solar panels

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 362 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: TESS uses four wide-angle cameras to watch most of the sky for tiny dips in starlight caused by orbiting planets. It focuses on bright, nearby stars, so other telescopes like Webb can follow up on the planets it finds. It took over the planet-hunting job from Kepler.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: TESS's orbit is timed with the Moon: it goes around Earth twice for every one lunar orbit.

craft.name: Viking Lander
craft.subtitle: The first US spacecraft to land and work on Mars

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Viking 1 and 2: Mars landers and orbiters

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Mission ended 1982 (Lander 1, last contact)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 3 m wide, 2 m tall

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 572 kg without fuel (657 kg fueled at launch)

facts.label: About
facts.value: Two Viking landers touched down on Mars in 1976 and sent back the first color pictures from its surface. They scooped up soil and ran experiments to test for life. The results were puzzling, and scientists still discuss them today.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Viking Lander 1 kept working for more than six years on Mars.

craft.name: Voyager
craft.subtitle: Twin probes now travelling between the stars

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Grand tour of the outer planets, now interstellar

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: 1977 (Voyager 1 and 2)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Both are still in contact from interstellar space. Since Nov. 14, 2026, Voyager 1 has sent only a basic radio signal and no data while engineers work on a computer problem.

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: high-gain antenna 3.7 m across; magnetometer boom 13 m

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 722 kg each at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: The twin Voyagers flew past Jupiter and Saturn, and Voyager 2 went on to Uranus and Neptune, the only spacecraft ever to visit them. Both have now left the Sun's bubble of solar wind and are in interstellar space. Each carries a golden record with sounds and images from Earth.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: In November 2026 Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth, so its radio signals take a full day to arrive.

facts.label: Real size

facts.value: The ISS circles Earth about every 90 minutes, about 400 km up. People have lived on board continuously since November 2000, running experiments on how space affects bodies, plants, and materials. It was built piece by piece over many years by five space agencies.

facts.value: The station and its crew are in free fall around Earth. That is why astronauts float, even though gravity there is still about 90% as strong as on the ground.

facts.value: NASA

facts.value: The Space Shuttle orbiter launched like a rocket and landed like a glider. It carried astronauts and large cargo, launched and repaired the Hubble Space Telescope, and helped build the ISS. Heat-resistant tiles on its belly protected it when it came back through the atmosphere.

craft.name: Gemini
craft.subtitle: The two-person capsule that practiced the moves for the Moon

facts.label: Mission

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: About
facts.value: Gemini carried two astronauts and was the bridge between Mercury and Apollo. Its crews practiced what a Moon trip would need: spacewalks, flights of up to two weeks, and meeting and docking with another spacecraft in orbit.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: In December 1965, Gemini 6A and Gemini 7 flew within about 30 cm (1 foot) of each other. It was the first time two crewed spacecraft met in orbit.

craft.name: Mercury Friendship 7
craft.subtitle: The capsule that carried John Glenn around Earth

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Mercury-Atlas 6: first American crewed orbital flight

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: February 20, 1962

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired after one flight (now at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: About 2.7 m (9 ft) tall and 1.9 m wide at the bottom, small enough that Glenn barely fit inside.

facts.value: John Glenn flew Friendship 7 around Earth three times in just under five hours. A warning signal suggested the heat shield might be loose, so he kept the retrorocket pack strapped on during reentry. The heat shield turned out to be fine.

facts.value: At each sunrise Glenn saw glowing specks drifting outside his window and called them fireflies. They turned out to be bits of frost from the capsule's small steering thrusters, which Scott Carpenter proved on the next flight by tapping the wall.

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.value: NASA

facts.value: Mars Exploration Rovers (two identical rovers)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.value: Opportunity drove 45.16 km (28.06 miles) on Mars. That was the record for driving on another world until Perseverance passed it in October 2026.

craft.name: Spitzer Space Telescope
craft.subtitle: Saw the universe in infrared, the light of heat

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Infrared space telescope, one of NASA's four Great Observatories

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL / Caltech

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: August 25, 2003

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired January 30, 2020

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: About 4 m (13 ft) tall.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 950 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Spitzer detected infrared light, which is heat, so it could see through dust clouds to find newborn stars and study planets around other stars. It had to stay very cold, so it trailed behind Earth in its own orbit around the Sun.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: In 2017 it helped reveal seven Earth-size planets around the star TRAPPIST-1.

craft.name: Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope
craft.subtitle: Watches the sky for the most energetic light in the universe
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Fermi Gamma-ray Large Area Space Telescope

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Gamma-ray observatory

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, U.S. Department of Energy, and partners in France, Germany, Italy, Japan and Sweden

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 2.9 m tall; solar panels 15 m tip to tip

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 4,303 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Gamma rays are the highest-energy form of light. Fermi scans the whole sky about every three hours, catching gamma-ray bursts, flaring black holes and spinning neutron stars called pulsars.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Fermi found two giant bubbles of gamma rays above and below the center of our Milky Way, each about 25,000 light-years tall.

craft.name: Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory
craft.subtitle: Raced to catch gamma-ray bursts, the biggest explosions in the universe

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Gamma-ray burst observatory

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, with partners in the UK and Italy

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: November 20, 2004

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Re-entered Earth's atmosphere November 4, 2026, after its orbit decayed

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 5.6 m tall; solar panels 4 m long

facts.label: About
facts.value: When Swift spotted a gamma-ray burst, it turned itself toward the burst in about a minute and a half, all on its own, to watch the fading afterglow in X-rays, ultraviolet and visible light. It also studied comets, exploding stars and black holes for almost 22 years.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It was named after the swift, a small bird that can turn quickly in flight.

craft.name: Terra
craft.subtitle: The flagship of NASA's Earth-watching satellites

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Earth Observing System flagship: land, oceans, air and energy balance

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, with instruments from Japan and Canada

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: December 18, 1999

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Ending: science data stops December 1, 2026; power-off planned January 2027 (as of Nov 17, 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: body 6.8 m long, 3.5 m across (about the size of a small school bus)

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 5,190 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Terra's instruments measure land, oceans, clouds, air pollution and Earth's energy balance at the same time. Designed for six years, it worked for 27, building a long record of wildfires, ice, forests and cities.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its MODIS camera images nearly the whole Earth every one to two days.

craft.name: Aqua
craft.subtitle: Tracks Earth's water: clouds, rain, ice and oceans

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Earth Observing System water-cycle mission

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, with instruments from Japan and Brazil

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Still working, but out of fuel for orbit boosts, so it is slowly drifting lower (as of November 2026).

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 4.8 m x 16.7 m x 8 m with its solar array out

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 2,934 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Aqua is named for water. It measures water vapor, clouds, rain, sea ice, snow and ocean temperatures, helping weather forecasters and climate scientists. It crosses the equator in the afternoon, so it sees places at a different time of day than Terra.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Aqua was designed to last six years and has been working for more than 24.

craft.name: Landsat 8
craft.subtitle: Part of the longest-running record of Earth's land from space

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Earth land-imaging satellite

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: February 11, 2013

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 4.9 m (16 ft) tall; solar array about 9.8 m (32 ft) long

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 2,780 kg (6,133 lb)

facts.label: About
facts.value: Landsat satellites have photographed Earth's land since 1972. Landsat 8 covers the whole planet every 16 days, so scientists can track crops, forests, glaciers, cities and wildfire scars over decades.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Each Landsat 8 scene covers a strip of ground about 185 km wide.

craft.name: SOHO
craft.subtitle: Has watched the Sun for three decades
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Solar and Heliospheric Observatory

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: ESA and NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: December 2, 1995

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 4.3 m tall; 9.5 m across its solar panels

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 1,850 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: SOHO sits about 1.5 million km from Earth, at a spot where it can see the Sun all the time. It studies the Sun's interior, its outer atmosphere and the solar wind, and it gives early warning of solar storms.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Although it was built to study the Sun, SOHO is the greatest comet finder in history. It passed 5,000 comets in 2024, most of them spotted by volunteers looking at its images.

craft.name: Stardust
craft.subtitle: Caught comet dust and brought it home

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Comet Wild 2 sample return

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: February 7, 1999

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired March 24, 2011 (sample capsule landed January 15, 2006)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: Its body was about 1.7 m tall, and its solar panels stretched 4.8 m tip to tip.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 385 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Stardust flew through the dust around comet Wild 2 in 2004 and caught tiny particles. Its capsule parachuted into Utah in 2006, the first time material from a comet was brought back to Earth.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It caught the dust in aerogel, one of the lightest solids ever made, which slowed the speeding grains gently, like a very soft catcher's mitt.

craft.name: Deep Impact
craft.subtitle: Fired an impactor into a comet to see what's inside

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Comet Tempel 1 impact, later extended as EPOXI

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: January 12, 2005

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Contact lost August 2013; mission ended September 2013

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: The flyby spacecraft was about 3.3 m long, 1.7 m wide and 2.3 m high.

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 973 kg at launch (601 kg flyby craft + 372 kg impactor)

facts.label: About
facts.value: On July 4, 2005, Deep Impact released a 372 kg impactor into the path of comet Tempel 1. The flyby spacecraft watched the crash, which blasted out a bright cloud of dust and ice and showed what the comet's surface was made of.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: The impactor hit the comet at about 10 km per second, or roughly 37,000 km/h.

craft.name: MESSENGER
craft.subtitle: The first spacecraft to orbit Mercury
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging (MESSENGER)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Mercury orbiter

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / Johns Hopkins APL

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: August 3, 2004

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Mission ended April 30, 2015 (crashed into Mercury as planned)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: body 1.27 m x 1.42 m x 1.85 m; sunshade about 2.5 m tall; 3.6 m magnetometer boom

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 1,108 kg at launch, more than half of it fuel

facts.label: About
facts.value: MESSENGER used flybys of Earth, Venus and Mercury to slow down enough to enter orbit around Mercury in March 2011. It mapped the whole planet and found evidence of water ice in polar craters that never see sunlight.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: A heat-resistant sunshade kept the spacecraft near room temperature while its sunny side faced up to about 370 C (700 F).

craft.name: 2001 Mars Odyssey
craft.subtitle: The longest-working spacecraft at Mars

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Mars orbiter: mapping and communications relay

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: April 7, 2001

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Odyssey has paused its science because one of the spinning wheels it uses to point itself stopped working. Engineers are testing it and hope to restart science in late November 2026.

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: body 2.2 m long, 1.7 m tall, 2.6 m wide; solar array 5.7 m

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 725 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Odyssey mapped the minerals of Mars and found large amounts of water ice just under the surface near the poles. For years it has also relayed messages between rovers on Mars and Earth.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It is named after the book and film 2001: A Space Odyssey.

craft.name: Solar Dynamics Observatory
craft.subtitle: Films the Sun in ultra-high definition
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Solar Dynamics Observatory (GitHub mirror)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Solar observatory studying the Sun's magnetic activity

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 4.5 m tall, 2.2 m wide; 6.25 m across its solar panels

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 3,100 kg at launch, fueled

facts.label: About
facts.value: SDO photographs the whole Sun in several colors of light about every 10 seconds. It tracks sunspots, flares and the Sun's magnetic field to help scientists understand and predict space weather.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: SDO sends back about 1.5 terabytes of data every day.

craft.name: STEREO
craft.subtitle: Twin spacecraft that gave the first 3D views of solar storms
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Solar TErrestrial RElations Observatory (STEREO) (GitHub mirror)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (two spacecraft)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: October 25, 2006 (U.S. time)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: STEREO-A operating (as of Nov 2026); STEREO-B lost contact in 2014

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 1.14 m tall, 2.03 m deep, 6.47 m wide with solar arrays

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 620 kg each

facts.label: About
facts.value: The two STEREO spacecraft spread out ahead of and behind Earth in its orbit around the Sun. Seeing from two angles, they made 3D views of eruptions on the Sun, and in 2011 they let scientists see the entire Sun at once for the first time.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: STEREO-A has gone all the way around the Sun and caught up with Earth again from behind, passing Earth in 2023.

craft.name: Deep Space 1
craft.subtitle: Proved that ion engines work in deep space

facts.label: Mission

facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Status

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 486 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Deep Space 1 tested 12 new technologies, including an ion engine that used electricity to push out xenon gas. It then flew past asteroid Braille and comet Borrelly and took close-up pictures of the comet's core.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its ion engine ran for more than 16,000 hours, a record at the time.

craft.name: NEAR Shoemaker

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 805 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: NEAR orbited asteroid 433 Eros for a year and mapped its rocky, cratered surface. It was not built to land, but on February 12, 2001 the team set it down gently on Eros, and it kept sending data from the surface for about two more weeks.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It was renamed in honor of Eugene Shoemaker, a planetary geologist famous for studying impact craters.

craft.name: LADEE
craft.subtitle: Studied the Moon's thin atmosphere and floating dust

facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Status

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 2.37 m tall, 1.85 m wide

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 383 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: The Moon has an extremely thin atmosphere called an exosphere. LADEE flew low over the Moon to sample it and to check whether dust floats above the surface. It also tested sending data by laser.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its laser link sent data from the Moon at 622 megabits per second, a record for laser communication from that distance at the time.

craft.name: Explorer 1
craft.subtitle: America's first satellite, on its Juno I rocket

facts.label: Mission

facts.value: Explorer 1 was a slim tube riding on top of the rocket's last stage. Its cosmic-ray instrument, built by James Van Allen's team, found belts of trapped radiation around Earth, now called the Van Allen belts.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: The satellite stayed joined to the rocket's small last stage, so the whole 2 m piece circled Earth together.

craft.name: Compton Gamma Ray Observatory

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Mass

facts.label: About
facts.value: Compton carried four instruments that covered a huge range of gamma-ray energies. It found that gamma-ray bursts come from all directions in the sky, a clue that they happen in faraway galaxies rather than in our own.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: At about 16,300 kg, it was the heaviest astrophysics payload the Space Shuttle had carried up to that time.

craft.name: WMAP
craft.subtitle: Measured the age of the universe from the Big Bang's afterglow
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP)

facts.value: Mapping the cosmic microwave background

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Status

facts.value: 3.8 m tall; 5.0 m wide across its sunshield

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 840 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: WMAP mapped the cosmic microwave background, faint heat left over from the early universe, across the whole sky. Its measurements pinned the age of the universe at about 13.77 billion years and showed how much of it is normal matter, dark matter and dark energy.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It worked about 1.5 million km from Earth, on the side away from the Sun, where it could stay shaded and very cold.

craft.name: Aquarius / SAC-D
craft.subtitle: Measured how salty the ocean surface is, from space

facts.value: Ocean surface salinity mapping (Aquarius instrument on Argentina's SAC-D satellite)

facts.label: Agency

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 1,350 kg at launch (2,977 lb)

facts.label: About
facts.value: Aquarius used microwave radiometers to sense how salty the top layer of the ocean is. Salt changes how dense seawater is, so the maps help explain ocean currents, rain and evaporation.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It could detect a change of about 0.2 grams of salt in a kilogram of seawater, roughly a pinch of salt in a gallon of water.

craft.name: Aura

facts.label: Mass

craft.name: CALIPSO

facts.value: Cloud and aerosol profiling with lidar

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and CNES (France)

craft.name: CloudSat
craft.subtitle: Used radar to look inside clouds

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Cloud-profiling radar mission

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, with the Canadian Space Agency

craft.name: CYGNSS
craft.subtitle: Eight small satellites that measure hurricane winds
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS)

facts.value: Ocean surface wind speed in tropical storms, using reflected GPS signals

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Seven of eight still flying; planned to be brought down around January 1, 2027 (as of Nov 2026; recheck)

facts.label: Mass

craft.name: DSCOVR

facts.value: It was built in the 1990s as Triana, sat in storage for about 8 years, and finally launched in 2015.

craft.name: Earth Observing-1

facts.value: Technology test for future Landsat-type imagers (New Millennium Program)

facts.value: NASA

craft.name: GOES weather satellite

facts.value: From that height, one satellite can see about 40% of the Earth at once.

craft.name: GRACE
craft.subtitle: Twin satellites that weighed Earth's water

facts.value: Mapping Earth's gravity changes caused by moving water and ice

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and the German Aerospace Center (DLR)

facts.label: Launch

craft.name: ICESat-2

craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Ice, Clouds, and Land Elevation Satellite-2 (ICESat-2) (B)

facts.value: NASA

craft.name: Jason-1

facts.value: Ocean surface height (radar altimetry)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and CNES (France)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: December 7, 2001

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Decommissioned July 1, 2013

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: body about 1 m across with two solar wings

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 500 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Jason-1 bounced radar pulses off the sea and timed the echoes to map ocean height. Bumps and dips in sea level reveal currents, El Nino and global sea level rise.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It was named after Jason, the hero of the Greek myth who sailed with the Argonauts.

craft.name: OSTM/Jason-2
craft.subtitle: Kept the sea-level record going after Jason-1
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Ocean Surface Topography Mission (OSTM Jason-2)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Ocean surface height (radar altimetry)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, NOAA, CNES and EUMETSAT

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Decommissioned October 9, 2019

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: body about 1 m across with two solar wings

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 510 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Jason-2 continued the sea-level measurements started by TOPEX/Poseidon in 1992. Together the missions show global sea level rising by about 3 mm a year over that time.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its radar measured the height of the sea surface from about 1,336 km up.

craft.name: Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich

craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Jason Continuity of Service (Sentinel-6)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Ocean surface height (radar altimetry)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, ESA, EUMETSAT, NOAA and CNES

facts.value: November 21, 2020

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 1,192 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich continues the sea-level record that began in 1992. It maps 95% of the world's ice-free ocean every 10 days.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It is named after Michael Freilich, a former director of NASA's Earth Science Division.

craft.name: Landsat 1
craft.subtitle: The first satellite built to photograph Earth's land

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Earth land imaging (first Landsat)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired January 6, 1978

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 3 m tall and 1.5 m wide; about 4 m across the solar paddles

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 950 kg (2,100 lb)

facts.label: About
facts.value: Landsat 1 started a record of Earth's land that continues today. Its pictures showed farms, forests, cities and floods from space, and were used to map places that had never been mapped well.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It was first called ERTS-1, the Earth Resources Technology Satellite. One of its images led to the discovery of a new island off Canada, named Landsat Island.

craft.name: Landsat 4
craft.subtitle: Brought the sharper Thematic Mapper camera

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Earth land imaging

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA, then NOAA

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Retired June 15, 2001; re-entered the atmosphere October 8, 2025 (recheck)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 4.3 m long

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 1,941 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Landsat 4 added the Thematic Mapper, which saw Earth in seven bands of light at 30 m detail. Its twin, Landsat 5, used the same design and kept working for almost 29 years.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Landsat 5, built to the same design, holds the Guinness record for the longest-operating Earth-observing satellite.

craft.name: Landsat 7
craft.subtitle: Landsat's workhorse for a quarter century

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Earth land imaging

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and the U.S. Geological Survey

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: April 15, 1999

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Decommissioned; last contact June 4, 2025

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 2.7 m x 2.7 m x 4.0 m

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 1,973 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Landsat 7 imaged the whole Earth every 16 days for 26 years. Its pictures track forests, farms, glaciers and growing cities.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: In 2003 a part that keeps its image lines straight broke, leaving diagonal gaps in its pictures. Scientists learned to fill the gaps and kept using its data for 22 more years.

craft.name: OCO-2
craft.subtitle: Measures carbon dioxide in the air from space

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Measuring carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: July 2, 2014

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026; recheck)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 2.1 m tall and 0.9 m wide when folded for launch

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 454 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: OCO-2 measures how sunlight reflected from Earth is absorbed by carbon dioxide. Its maps show where carbon dioxide is released and where forests and oceans soak it up.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It replaced the first OCO, which was lost in 2009 when its rocket's nose cover failed to come off.

craft.name: POES weather satellite
craft.subtitle: Polar-orbiting weather satellites that circle over both poles
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Polar Operational Environmental Satellite (POES)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Polar-orbiting weather and climate observations

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NOAA, with NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: TIROS-N series from 1978; NOAA-19 (last) in 2009

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Series retired; NOAA-19 decommissioned in 2025 (recheck)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: body 4.19 m long, 1.88 m wide; 7.4 m with the solar array

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 1,420 kg at launch (NOAA-19)

facts.label: About
facts.value: POES satellites flew pole to pole, so each one saw the whole planet twice a day. Their data fed weather forecasts and built a long climate record.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: They also carried search-and-rescue receivers that picked up distress beacons from ships and planes.

craft.name: QuikSCAT
craft.subtitle: Measured winds over the ocean with a spinning radar

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Ocean surface winds (radar scatterometer)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Antenna stopped spinning November 23, 2009; spacecraft decommissioned in 2018 (recheck)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: spacecraft body 2.2 m x 1.7 m x 1.4 m

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 970 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: QuikSCAT's spinning dish sent radar pulses to the sea. Wind makes small ripples, and the strength of the echo revealed wind speed and direction, even under clouds.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It was built in about a year, very fast for a NASA satellite, to replace NASA's NSCAT wind sensor, lost when the Japanese satellite carrying it failed in 1997.

craft.name: RADARSAT-1
craft.subtitle: Canada's radar satellite that saw through clouds and darkness

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Synthetic aperture radar imaging of Earth

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: Canadian Space Agency, launched by NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: November 4, 1995

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Ended March 29, 2013

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: radar antenna 15 m x 1.5 m

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 2,750 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: RADARSAT-1 made images with radar, so it could see the ground day or night and through clouds. It mapped sea ice, floods and crops, and made the first complete radar map of Antarctica in 1997.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: NASA launched it in exchange for data, including that Antarctic mapping campaign.

craft.name: SAC-C
craft.subtitle: Argentina's Earth-watching satellite, launched by NASA
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Satellite for Scientific Applications (SAC-C)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Earth imaging and magnetic field studies

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: CONAE (Argentina), NASA and partners

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: November 21, 2000 (with EO-1)

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Ended August 15, 2013

facts.label: Real size

facts.label: Mass

facts.label: About
facts.value: SAC-C flew in formation with Landsat 7 and EO-1 to compare cameras, and carried instruments that measured Earth's magnetic field and used GPS signals to study the atmosphere.

facts.value: It shared its rocket with NASA's EO-1.

craft.name: SeaStar (SeaWiFS)
craft.subtitle: Mapped ocean color to track the plankton that feed the sea

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Ocean color imaging with the SeaWiFS sensor

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: Orbital Sciences, with NASA buying the science data

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: August 1, 1997

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Contact lost December 2010

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: a small satellite, about 3 m across with its solar panels

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 300 to 390 kg (sources differ)

facts.label: About
facts.value: SeaWiFS measured the color of the ocean. Greener water has more phytoplankton, tiny plants that make about half the oxygen produced on Earth.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It was the first commercial satellite NASA bought science data from instead of building its own.

craft.name: Suomi NPP
craft.subtitle: Bridged the old weather satellites and the new JPSS fleet
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (Suomi NPP)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Polar-orbiting weather and climate observations

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and NOAA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: October 28, 2011

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Stopped sending data November 2, 2026; NOAA plans to lower it for re-entry over the South Pacific from December 1 to about December 12, 2026 (recheck)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 1.3 m x 1.3 m x 4.2 m body

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 2,128 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Suomi NPP tested the instruments now used on NOAA's JPSS weather satellites and fed daily forecasts for years. Its VIIRS camera made the famous Black Marble images of Earth's city lights at night.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It is named after Verner Suomi, often called the father of satellite meteorology.

craft.name: TOPEX/Poseidon
craft.subtitle: Started the satellite record of global sea level

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Ocean surface height (radar altimetry)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and CNES (France)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: August 10, 1992

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Ended January 2006

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 5.5 m long, 6.6 m tall, 2.8 m wide; 11.5 m with the solar array

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 2,388 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: TOPEX/Poseidon measured sea level across the globe every 10 days. It mapped ocean currents and tides and watched the giant 1997 El Nino form in the Pacific.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It worked for more than 13 years, over four times its 3-year design life.

craft.name: TOMS Earth Probe
craft.subtitle: Kept watch on the ozone hole in the 1990s
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Total Ozone Mapping Spectrometer (TOMS)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Mapping total ozone with the TOMS instrument

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: July 2, 1996

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Ended December 2006 (recheck)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 1.2 m wide, 1.8 m tall; 3.9 m across the solar panels

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: about 295 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: TOMS measured how much ultraviolet sunlight Earth's atmosphere scatters back to space, which reveals how much ozone is overhead. It kept watching the Antarctic ozone hole each spring.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Earlier TOMS instruments first mapped the ozone hole from space in the 1980s.

craft.name: TRMM
craft.subtitle: Measured tropical rain from space for 17 years
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Tropical Rainfall Measuring Mission (TRMM)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Measuring rainfall in the tropics, including the first rain radar in space

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and JAXA (Japan)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: November 27, 1997

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Science ended April 2015; re-entered June 16, 2015

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: body about 5.1 m long, 3.7 m wide

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 3,620 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: TRMM carried the first radar in space built to measure rain. It looked inside hurricanes and showed how much rain falls in the tropics, where about two thirds of Earth's rain falls.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It was designed for three years and worked for more than 17.

craft.name: ACRIMSAT
craft.subtitle: A small satellite that measured the Sun's brightness
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Active Cavity Irradiance Monitor Satellite (AcrimSAT) (A)

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Measuring total solar energy reaching Earth

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA / JPL

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: December 21, 1999

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Last contact December 14, 2013

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: 77.5 cm wide, 66 cm high; 1.78 m across the solar panels

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 115 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: ACRIMSAT measured the total sunlight arriving at Earth very precisely. Small changes in the Sun's output matter for understanding climate.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: It rode to orbit as the second passenger on a Taurus rocket, tucked under Korea's KOMPSAT satellite.

craft.name: AIM
craft.subtitle: Studied glowing night clouds at the edge of space
craft.sourceLabel: NASA 3D Resources: Aeronomy of Ice in the Mesosphere

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Studying noctilucent (night-shining) clouds about 80 km up

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: April 25, 2007

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Ended March 13, 2023; re-entered August 19, 2024

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 1.4 m x 1.1 m body

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 197 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: Noctilucent clouds are the highest clouds on Earth, made of ice crystals near the edge of space. AIM showed how they form and why they have become more common.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: These clouds can only be seen from the ground just after sunset or before sunrise, when the Sun still lights them from below the horizon.

craft.name: GPM Core Observatory
craft.subtitle: Measures rain and snow around the globe

facts.label: Mission
facts.value: Global rain and snow measurement (successor to TRMM)

facts.label: Agency
facts.value: NASA and JAXA (Japan)

facts.label: Launch
facts.value: February 27, 2014

facts.label: Status
facts.value: Operating (as of Nov 2026; recheck)

facts.label: Real size
facts.value: about 13 m x 6.5 m x 5 m with its solar arrays out

facts.label: Mass
facts.value: 3,850 kg at launch

facts.label: About
facts.value: GPM's radar and microwave imager measure rain and snow, from light drizzle to heavy downpours. It anchors a fleet of satellites that together map precipitation every 30 minutes.

facts.label: Fun fact
facts.value: Its radar can see inside storms in three dimensions, slicing through clouds like a CT scan.
